Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
I work hard at keeping busy with other things

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Samir, a 48-year-old fashion designer of Middle Eastern descent, had built his career on precision and sensory awareness-the weight of a fabric, the exact shade of a dye, the way light fell on a seam. That same attunement became his undoing on the afternoon of the warehouse fire. He had been inspecting a new collection of silk garments when a faulty electrical panel exploded, sending a wave of heat and acrid smoke through the space. In the chaos that followed, he remembered only fragments: the taste of copper and burnt polyester flooding his mouth, the nauseating sensation of his own skin suddenly feeling scorching hot, and then disconnected images-a falling beam, someone's scream, the cold concrete of the loading dock where he finally collapsed. What stayed with him most was how the memory refused to stay in the past. When it came, it did not feel like recollection; it felt like the fire was happening again, right there in his showroom or his apartment, and he could taste the metal and smoke on his tongue.

In the months that followed, Samir found that certain moments would ambush him without warning. A sudden spike in temperature-the heat of a pressing iron, or even a warm breeze through an open window-would trigger the memory of that burning skin, and with it came a wave of nausea that doubled him over. These intrusions made the world feel permanently unsafe. He began scanning every room he entered for exits, mapping escape routes before he could sit down, and his concentration fractured; he would lose track of a client's measurements mid-sentence because his mind was already checking the door. The more the memories intruded, the more vigilant he became, and the more vigilant he became, the more the memories surfaced-a tightening loop he could not break. When the fear became unbearable, he took a razor blade to his forearm, just to feel something other than the heat and the dread. The sharp, clean pain was a release, a way to ground himself in the present, but afterward the shame of it would circle back, feeding the memory of the fire all over again.

To manage the constant threat he felt, Samir threw himself into work, keeping his schedule so packed that there was no room for silence. He would stay late at the studio, pinning fabrics and sketching until his eyes burned, and then return home only to check the locks on his doors and windows three, four, sometimes five times before bed. The busyness helped for a while-it drowned out the intrusive tastes and the fragmented images-but it also exhausted him, and when he finally slowed down, the memories hit harder, as if they had been waiting. He had come to believe that the only way to stay safe was to never stop moving, never let his guard down, and never let himself feel the full weight of what had happened. But the vigilance itself was wearing him out, and the checking and the cutting were no longer enough to hold the fire at bay. What finally brought Samir to seek help was a moment in his own showroom, during a fitting with a longtime client. The steam from the iron drifted across his face, and suddenly he was back on the loading dock, tasting smoke, his hands shaking so badly he had to excuse himself. He knew then that he could not design his way out of this. He was terrified that the memories would never stop, that the vigilance would consume the last part of him that still felt like a creator rather than a survivor, but he was even more afraid of what might happen if he did not try.
